sources.title: Phan Châu Trinh (Q2705303), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'Phan Châu Trinh', description 'Vietnamese nationalist in the 20th century', Chinese label 潘周楨, Korean label 판쩌우찐 and a Korean Wikipedia article of that title, instance of human, born 9 September 1872, died 23 March 1926 (the scholarly sources read give 24 March), citizenship Vietnam, occupations including politician and writer. Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Sophie Quinn-Judge, review of Vinh Sinh (ed. and trans.), Phan Chu Trinh and His Political Writings (Cornell Southeast Asia Program, 2009), Journal of the Siam Society 99 (2011), pp. 320-325 (read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE (through a scholarly review): treats him as one of the two great Vietnamese scholar-nationalists of the early twentieth century and, after Vinh Sinh, as the earliest and most eloquent Vietnamese proponent of democracy, who sought non-violent self-rule through cultural change and political modernisation. Covers his 1904 withdrawal from the mandarinate, the 1905 fact-finding trip and the school and fish-sauce factory it produced, the 1906 trip to China and Japan, his role in the Dong Kinh Free School and in hair-cutting and Western dress, his letter of warning to Governor-General Beau, the arrest after the 1908 tax protests with a commuted death sentence, the 1910 amnesty won by French socialists, his move to Paris in 1911, the 1912 association with Phan Van Truong, the Sante prison from September 1914 to July 1915, the post-war appeal drafted with Phan Van Truong and Nguyen Ai Quoc, his 1925 return, two final Saigon lectures and a funeral of about 16,000; notes that critics call him a collaborator naive about French intentions and that he may have exaggerated his differences with Phan Boi Chau for the French. Scholarly review of a translation volume; draws on Marr and on Huynh Thuc Khang's memoir.

Dinh Xuan Lam, 'Phan Chau Trinh: life and career', VNU Journal of Science: Social Sciences and Humanities 22(5E), 2006 (English-language article for the 80th anniversary of his death; read in full). Vietnamese state-historiography biography, admiring: his resignation from office, the 1906 meeting with Phan Boi Chau where he criticised uprisings and reliance on foreign aid, his opposition to the monarchy, the 1908 arrest and Con Dao exile, the 1911 move to France after an amnesty won through the Human Rights League, the 1914-15 imprisonment on suspicion of ties to Germany, the 1919 claims, his 18 February 1922 letter to Nguyen Ai Quoc, the July 1922 open letter against Emperor Khai Dinh, his May 1925 request to return, his Saigon talks against monarchy, his telephone appeals about an amnesty for Phan Boi Chau and against choosing a successor to Khai Dinh, and his death on 24 March 1926. Draws on Fourniau, Thu Trang and Nguyen Phan Quang.

'The "Affair of the Tombs," 1912-1913', Historic Vietnam (compilation of period newspaper reports; read in full). Includes the Annales coloniales article of 6 May 1913 summarising an interview Phan Châu Trinh gave to the Paris daily Le Journal (journalist Fernand Hauser): he said he had warned a friend by letter before the Hanoi bombing of 26 April 1913, that he loved France and hoped it would grant reforms, and that the oppressive regime was like wood piled at a hearth. The colonial-press author is hostile, calls his words a veiled threat, and says he had been sentenced to death in 1907, pardoned, held three years on Poulo Condor and released after Maurice Viollette intervened (scholars date the sentence to 1908). Adversarial French colonial press of 1913, reproduced by a modern history website.

Phan-Châu-Trinh lịch-sử: Quốc gia huyết lệ (Saigon: Thịnh-Quang, printed by Xưa-Nay, 1926; 32 pages, illustrated; preface by Nguyễn Ngọc Sơn dated 8 April 1926), Bibliothèque nationale de France 8-INDOCH PIECE-396, digitised on Gallica (read as page images: the biography on pages 3-7 at legible resolution; the cover, preface, funeral reports with photographs credited to Khánh Ký, tributes and poems only as smaller, partly legible images). Contemporary Vietnamese-language funeral booklet issued within weeks of his death: hagiographic; used for the cover portrait and as a consistency check on the outline of his life (1872 birth, degrees in 1901-02, lectures at the Dong Kinh school in June 1907, a hunger strike after arrest, sentence to Con Lon in April 1908 and nearly three years there, departure for France given as 1912 where scholars give 1911, Sante prison September 1914 to August 1915, an open letter charging the visiting emperor with seven crimes dated there to 1924, return in June 1925, two Saigon lectures, death on 24 March 1926); a secondary support in two rows, never the sole support.

Quốc gia huyết lệ, volume 2: Đầu chánh phủ thơ (Saigon: Thịnh-Quang, 1926; 37 pages), Bibliothèque nationale de France 8-INDOCH-20, Gallica (read: cover, publisher's notes, title page and the opening of the letter). Reprints Phan Châu Trinh's letter to Governor-General Beau dated 2 April 1907, which begins by calling the state of the country critical and names the abuses of officialdom, the sickness of civil life and the rot of customs. A 1926 reissue of a primary text, used only for the date and the gist of the letter.

VietnamNet (English), 'The forgotten patriot behind Vietnamese photography: Nguyen Dinh Khanh' (read in full): the Saigon photographer Khánh Ký was a trusted friend of Phan Châu Trinh for over a decade in France and in the last two years of his life in Saigon, photographed the whole 1926 funeral and compiled a memorial album. Used only for the photographer's relationship to the sitter.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_pct_quinn, src_pct_dinh, src_pct_tombs, src_pct_gallica1926b, src_pct_gallica1926 | 1907-1925 | scholarly review, historian's article, 1913 colonial press, 1926 reprint of his letter, 1926 funeral booklet] He wrote to Governor-General Beau on 2 April 1907 attacking the abuses of the mandarin system; told a Paris daily in 1913 that the colonial regime was storing up trouble, which a hostile colonial paper called a veiled threat; made public charges against Emperor Khai Dinh in 1922 (the 1926 booklet also reports the letter but dates it 1924); and gave Saigon talks against monarchy in 1925, after two imprisonments. Four instances from scholarly, state-historiography and adversarial-press families. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 74 / 0.62 to 72 / 0.6 because the 1922 letter rests on one historian and a eulogy that misdates it, and only the opening of the 1907 letter was read. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 70 / 0.58 because he framed the appeals as requests to the colonial power, which limits how confrontational the conduct was.

persistence.rationale: [src_pct_quinn, src_pct_dinh, src_pct_gallica1926 | 1904-1926 | scholarly review, historian's article, 1926 funeral booklet] After resigning as a mandarin in 1904 he kept to the reform line through the 1908 arrest and nearly three years on Con Dao, the 1914-15 Sante imprisonment, the loss of his stipend and about fourteen years of surveillance in France, and in 1925 returned to Saigon and gave public lectures in his last months. Documented across several sources; the two main ones share Vietnamese historiographic sources. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.58 to 68 / 0.56. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 66 / 0.54 for martyrdom bias in the admiring sources.

proactive_agency.rationale: [src_pct_quinn, src_pct_dinh | 1905-1912 | scholarly review, historian's article] Without being asked he made a fact-finding trip to the south in 1905 that led to a modern school and a fish-sauce factory, travelled to China and Japan in 1906, helped found the Dong Kinh Free School, formed societies for new learning and public speaking, persuaded the French in 1911 to let him go to Paris to lobby, and in 1912 co-founded an association of Vietnamese patriots. Initiative is documented, but the two sources overlap and the organisational results were limited. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 70 / 0.58 to 68 / 0.54. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 66 / 0.52 because credit for the southern programme is shared with Tran Quy Cap and Huynh Thuc Khang.

impact_motivation.rationale: [src_pct_quinn, src_pct_dinh, src_pct_tombs | 1904-1926 | scholarly review, historian's article, 1913 colonial press] He left an official career, accepted prison and exile, and pressed throughout for schools, civil rights and an end to monarchy; the hostile 1913 report shows him putting the same reform demands to a Paris audience. His aims are stated in his own writings and documented by independent scholars. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 76 / 0.62 to 72 / 0.58 because the admiring Vietnamese sources tell the aim in the same terms. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 70 / 0.56 because the aim is inferred from conduct that the sources also praise.

independent_thinking.rationale: [src_pct_quinn, src_pct_dinh | 1904-1925 | scholarly review, historian's article] He left the mandarinate in 1904 and by 1906 told Phan Boi Chau that neither uprising nor reliance on foreign help would work, a position that also divided him from his best-known contemporary; he argued that monarchy should end and that rights should come before independence, a view critics call naive about French intentions. His reading was largely Chinese and Japanese reformist writing, so the independence is in his conclusions rather than his sources. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 68 / 0.56 to 66 / 0.52. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 64 / 0.5 because Quinn-Judge suspects he may have exaggerated his differences with Phan Boi Chau for the French.

belief_updating.rationale: [src_pct_quinn, src_pct_dinh | 1904-1925 | scholarly review, historian's article] The two historians describe a move from the examination route to reformist modernisation in 1904 and, after years in France, growing disillusion with French colonial policy by 1925, with a 1922 letter to Nguyen Ai Quoc that Quinn-Judge says encouraged the younger man to take Marxist ideas to Vietnam; he never joined the communists, and the changes are summarised by historians rather than shown in his own words. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 60 / 0.48 to 56 / 0.44. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 54 / 0.4 because both summaries describe a drift, not a documented reversal.

collaboration.rationale: [src_pct_quinn, src_pct_dinh | 1905-1919 | scholarly review, historian's article] He worked with Tran Quy Cap and Huynh Thuc Khang on the reform programme, formed an association with Phan Van Truong in 1912, lived and worked alongside Nguyen Ai Quoc in Paris, and drafted the 1919 appeal for Vietnamese rights with them. Several partnerships are documented, but only in summary and credit within them is hard to apportion. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.5 strong inference to 60 / 0.48 inference because the partnerships are listed in summary form by two overlapping sources. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 58 / 0.46 because the partnerships were also political alignments of convenience in exile.

persuasiveness.rationale: [src_pct_quinn, src_pct_dinh | 1911-1925 | scholarly review, historian's article] He persuaded the French authorities in 1911 to let him go to Paris, lobbied the Socialist Party, the Human Rights League and the press, drew packed audiences in Saigon in 1925, and telephoned the Governor-General about an amnesty for Phan Boi Chau; but Dinh describes the 1911 permission as a French wish to isolate him, and no result of the lobbying is documented. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.48 to 58 / 0.44. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 56 / 0.42 for outcome ambiguity.

risk_tolerance.rationale: [src_pct_quinn, src_pct_dinh, src_pct_tombs, src_pct_gallica1926 | 1907-1925 | scholarly review, historian's article, 1913 colonial press, 1926 funeral booklet] He addressed the colonial government and later the monarchy openly while French agents watched him; he was imprisoned after 1908 (though he denied involvement) and again in 1914, and in 1925 he returned to speak publicly. His acceptance of danger is inferred from repeated public acts; the sources do not report how he weighed the risks. CONCENTRATION CHECK (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.5 strong inference to 58 / 0.46 inference. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered to 56 / 0.44 because the 1908 arrest followed events he denied taking part in, so it was not a chosen risk.

portrait.source: Studio portrait of Phan Châu Trinh, seated in a dark suit and bow tie, a print with a partly legible embossed studio imprint at the foot that reads '...NH KY & Cie ... Bonnard ... Saigon' (consistent with Khánh Ký's Saigon studio; the first letters are not legible, so the credit is a reading, not a printed name). The shipped file is a scan of that original print (1280 x 2037, from the Wikimedia Commons file Phan Chau Trinh.jpg, which took it from a personal website, not from a library), cropped by a few pixels and reduced to 623 x 1000; no upscaling. The same exposure (identical pose, collar, bow tie, hands, chair and painted backdrop), in a tighter crop that omits the studio imprint, was printed as the cover portrait of the Saigon booklet Phan-Châu-Trinh lịch-sử: Quốc gia huyết lệ (Thịnh-Quang, 1926; preface dated 8 April 1926; Bibliothèque nationale de France 8-INDOCH PIECE-396, Gallica ark:/12148/bpt6k4236248g, catalogued 'domaine public'), which fixes a documented first publication before 1931. The BnF digitisation was used only as proof of publication and was not reused.
portrait.license: Public domain: the photograph was published in Saigon in 1926 (before 1931), so it is in the public domain in the United States; the studio print bears a Khánh Ký studio imprint and Khánh Ký (1874-1946) died more than 70 years ago; the shipped scan does not come from Gallica, whose conditions make commercial reuse of its own digitisations licensed and paid
portrait.attribution: Studio portrait of Phan Châu Trinh by the Khánh Ký studio, Saigon (imprint partly legible), before April 1926; scan via Wikimedia Commons (cropped and reduced). First publication: cover of Phan-Châu-Trinh lịch-sử: Quốc gia huyết lệ (Saigon: Thịnh-Quang, 1926), Bibliothèque nationale de France.
portrait.creator: Khánh Ký (Nguyễn Đình Khánh, 1874-1946) studio, Saigon, by a partly legible studio imprint; the 1926 booklet does not credit the cover portrait
portrait.date: before April 1926 (undated print; first documented publication on the cover of a Saigon booklet of April-May 1926)

provenance.notes: portrait_preflight: Stage B grade plausible. Lead: Commons 'Phan Chau Trinh.jpg' (PD-Vietnam, author Khánh Ký) with an undocumented first publication. LEAD SURVIVED, now documented: (1) the print itself carries an embossed studio imprint at the foot, partly legible as '...NH KY & Cie / ... Bonnard / ... Saigon', i.e. consistent with Khánh Ký's studio; the first letters are lost, so this is a reading; (2) I found the same exposure (compared side by side: pose, collar, bow tie, hands, chair, backdrop), in a tighter crop without the imprint, printed as the cover portrait of 'Phan-Châu-Trinh lịch-sử: Quốc gia huyết lệ' (Saigon: Thịnh-Quang, printed by Xưa-Nay, 1926, price 0$30, depot-legal stamp, preface dated 8 April 1926), BnF 8-INDOCH PIECE-396, digitised on Gallica (ark:/12148/bpt6k4236248g, catalogued 'domaine public'), so first publication is documented before 1931 (US public domain). The cover is a coarse halftone and carries no credit; inside, the funeral photographs are credited 'Photo Khánh-Ký'. Sitter: the cover title names him; the portrait matches the studio print (same pose, bow tie, hands) which the Commons file and the Hum@zur record (Université Côte d'Azur, Fonds ASEMI, item 22220 'Phan Chu Trinh (1872-1926)', creator Nguyễn Đình Khánh, rights 'Domaine public') both identify as him; the Hum@zur record says it is a photograph of a photograph and points to Commons as 'identical to', so it is not independent of Commons. Khánh Ký was a friend and photographer of Phan Châu Trinh (VietnamNet). HOLDER TERMS: Gallica's conditions (read, 13/12/2021): non-commercial reuse of its contents is free with a source credit; COMMERCIAL REUSE OF GALLICA CONTENT IS PAID AND LICENSED. I therefore did NOT ship a Gallica-derived file: the shipped scan is the Commons-hosted scan of the original studio print (non-BnF origin, a personal website), and Gallica is used only as documentary proof of the 1926 publication. The Gallica ark pages and thumbnails returned a Cloudflare challenge (recorded as a bot wall, not bypassed); the pages were read through the Gallica IIIF image API, which answered normally. Lead decision for the risk: if you treat the BnF conditions as covering any reproduction of the 1926 cover, the shipped file is unaffected because it is not from the BnF copy. The Commons PD-Vietnam tag was NOT relied on. KIND likeness (a lifetime studio photograph). Quality: 623 x 1000 from a 1280 x 2037 scan, not upscaled; the print has a brown cast and an embossed imprint across the lower right. Photo date unknown; Phan returned to Saigon in 1925 and the booklet is of April 1926, so the sitter is probably in his early fifties, but that is inference. REGION south_asia (Southeast Asian precedent). KOREAN NAME 판쩌우찐 is the Wikidata ko label and Korean Wikipedia title. SCOPE: scored only on documented conduct (resignation in 1904, the reform programme, letters and lectures, prison and exile, the Paris years); the 1913 Hanoi bombing and the 1908 tax protests are not attributed to him (he denied involvement and the sources differ). The death sentence is dated 1908 by the scholars and 1907 by the 1913 colonial paper; death 23 March (Wikidata) or 24 March 1926 (scholars and the 1926 booklet); departure for France 1911 (scholars) or 1912 (booklet); the open letter to the emperor 1922 (Dinh) or 1924 (booklet). The critical 'collaborator' reading is noted in the sources and lowers the independent-thinking row's impact to dual-edged. READ (6 sources besides Wikidata): Quinn-Judge review (full), Dinh Xuan Lam (full), Historic Vietnam 1913 press compilation (full), the two 1926 Gallica booklets (volume 1 biography pages 3-7 at legible resolution, the rest as smaller images; volume 2 front matter and the opening of the letter), VietnamNet on Khánh Ký. Not read: Marr, Vinh Sinh's translations, Huynh Thuc Khang's 1959 memoir, Thu Trang, the Japanese study of the Sante case, the Review of Politics article. CONCENTRATION: nine rows, all lowered; two moved from strong inference to inference; SELF-CALIBRATION lowered all nine further; raised 0.
